unit_label: Module A: International Banking - External Commercial Borrowings and Foreign Investments in India

facts.statement: Any person resident in India other than an individual, incorporated, established or registered under a Central or State Act, is an eligible ECB borrower if permitted to borrow externally under the applicable Act. A borrower under a restructuring scheme or corporate insolvency resolution process may raise ECB only if the plan specifically permits it. A borrower against whom an investigation, adjudication or appeal for contravention of FEMA is pending may still raise ECB, without prejudice to the outcome, but must disclose it in Form ECB 1 (or Revised Form ECB 1).

An eligible borrower may raise ECB from a person resident outside India, from a branch outside India of an entity whose lending business is regulated by the Reserve Bank, and from a financial institution or branch set up in an International Financial Services Centre.

ECB may be denominated in foreign currency or Indian rupees, and the currency may be changed from one foreign currency to another, from foreign currency to rupees and back, at the exchange rate on the date of the agreement or one that does not produce a higher liability. ECB may take any form of commercial borrowing involving agreed interest and repayment of principal, including FCCBs and FCEBs. Funds received from non-residents after 30 April 2007 against preference shares or debentures not fully and mandatorily convertible are ECB. Trade credit of original maturity up to three years, export advances, investments under the Debt Instruments and Non-Debt Instrument rules and FVCI debt investments are not ECB.

An eligible borrower may raise ECB up to the higher of (a) outstanding ECB up to USD 1 billion, or (b) total outstanding borrowing, external and domestic, up to 300 per cent of net worth as per the last audited standalone balance sheet. Outstanding borrowing excludes non-fund-based credit and funds raised through mandatorily convertible securities. The proposed ECB, other than for refinancing, counts towards the limit. The limit does not apply to borrowers regulated by financial sector regulators. All ECBs conforming to the Schedule can be raised under the automatic route; other cases go to the Reserve Bank under the approval route.
facts.locator: Schedule I, paragraphs 5; amended regulation on routes

facts.statement: The minimum average maturity period (MAMP) is three years. A manufacturing sector borrower may raise ECB with average maturity between one and three years if the outstanding amount of such ECBs does not exceed USD 150 million. Call and put options cannot be exercised before the MAMP is complete. MAMP need not be met on conversion into non-debt instruments, repayment from non-debt instrument proceeds on repatriation basis received after drawdown, refinance, waiver of debt by the lender, or repayment needed for corporate actions such as closure, merger or liquidation.

The cost of borrowing, defined as interest, other fees, expenses, charges, guarantee fees and export credit agency charges (but not commitment fees and statutory taxes payable in India), must be in line with prevailing market conditions. For an ECB with average maturity under three years the cost must comply with the ceiling for trade credit; in a fixed rate loan the floating rate plus spread of the corresponding swap must not exceed the ceiling. ECB from a related party must be on an arm's length basis. Prepayment charges and penal interest must be in line with market conditions.

Funds borrowed must not be used in India for chit funds, Nidhi companies, real estate business and construction of farmhouses (with specified exceptions for construction-development projects and industrial parks), agriculture and animal husbandry (with listed exceptions such as floriculture, horticulture, seeds, animal husbandry and aquaculture), plantation other than tea, coffee, rubber, cardamom, palm oil tree and olive oil tree, trading in transferable development rights, transacting in listed or unlisted securities (except specified corporate actions for strategic purposes), repayment of a domestic rupee loan that was used for a restricted end-use or is an NPA, and on-lending for any restricted purpose.

A borrower draws down ECB only after obtaining a Loan Registration Number (LRN) from the Reserve Bank through its designated AD Category I bank. ECB proceeds for rupee expenditure in India are credited to a rupee account in India with the designated bank by the end of the succeeding month and, pending use, may be placed in an unencumbered fixed deposit of up to one year; proceeds for foreign currency expenditure may be held in a foreign currency account in India or abroad and invested outside India in an unencumbered fixed deposit or debt instrument of original maturity up to one year.

ECB may be secured by a charge on immovable, movable, financial or intangible assets or by a guarantee under the Foreign Exchange Management (Guarantees) Regulations, 2026; the agreement must contain a clause requiring security, an existing lender's no objection certificate is needed before charging an encumbered asset, and RBI-regulated entities may not issue any type of guarantee. An existing ECB may be refinanced by a fresh ECB if the refinancing does not cause a failure to meet the MAMP applicable to the original borrowing. An ECB may be converted into a non-debt instrument under the Non-Debt Instruments Rules with no additional cost to the lender, the lender's consent, and consent of or information to other lenders. Principal, interest and charges may be remitted.

The borrower files Form ECB 1 through the designated bank to obtain the LRN; Revised Form ECB 1 within seven calendar days from the end of the month in which a change took effect; and Form ECB 2 within seven calendar days from the end of the month in which proceeds were received or debt servicing was undertaken. Late reporting may be regularised by paying a late submission fee. A borrower with an active LRN who fails to submit returns for four consecutive quarters after the quarter of a scheduled drawdown or servicing, and cannot be traced, is treated as untraceable and the bank informs the Reserve Bank and the Directorate of Enforcement if it happened after a drawdown.

Importers may raise trade credit from outside India, for import of capital and non-capital goods permitted under the Foreign Trade Policy and for purchases within an SEZ. Trade credit may be in any freely convertible currency or in rupees, up to USD 50 million equivalent per import transaction. The period from the date of shipment is up to one year linked to the operating cycle for non-capital goods and up to three years for capital goods. Recognised lenders are overseas suppliers, banks and financial institutions, foreign equity holders and financial institutions in IFSCs. Authorised dealers may issue bank guarantees in favour of the overseas supplier, bank or financial institution if the import and trade credit comply with the norms.

The courseware (S03 printed pp. 166-170) describes the earlier ECB framework: minimum average maturity of 3, 5, 7 or 10 years depending on the use, an all-in-cost ceiling of benchmark plus 500 bps (450 bps for rupee ECB), an automatic route limit of USD 750 million a year, a negative list including working capital and general corporate purposes except from a foreign equity holder, an ECB liability-equity ratio of 7:1 for foreign equity holder lending, and recognised lenders confined to FATF- or IOSCO-compliant countries.

payload.title: ECBs in 2026: the framework was rewritten in February
payload.core_explanation_md:
Older books (and some courseware sections) describe the ECB rules of **2018-2019**: maturity of 3, 5, 7 or 10 years by end-use, an **all-in-cost cap** (benchmark plus 500 bps), an automatic route of **USD 750 million** a year, and several lender and ratio rules.

On **9 February 2026** RBI amended the Borrowing and Lending Regulations (published in the Gazette on **16 February 2026**), **before** the 30 June 2026 cut-off. The result:
- **One maturity rule** (three years) with a manufacturing carve-out.
- **No all-in-cost cap**: cost follows **market conditions**.
- A **new borrowing limit**: the higher of **USD 1 billion** or **300% of net worth**.
- A **list of end-uses that are barred**, restated in one place.

ECBs registered **before** the change continue under the old rules, except for reporting. When a question quotes the old figures, it is testing the earlier framework.

payload.title: Who can borrow, from whom, in what currency
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Borrower**: any resident **non-individual** incorporated, established or registered under a **Central or State Act**, **if** the governing Act allows external borrowing.
- Under a **restructuring** or **insolvency resolution**: only if the plan **specifically permits** ECB.
- With an **investigation pending** for a FEMA contravention: **allowed**, without prejudice to the outcome, but it must be **disclosed in Form ECB 1**.

**Lender**: a **person resident outside India**; a **branch abroad of an entity whose lending RBI regulates**; or a **financial institution in an IFSC**.

**Currency**: **foreign currency or rupees**; the currency can be **switched** at the rate on the date of the agreement (or a rate giving no higher liability).

**Forms**: any commercial borrowing with agreed interest and repayment, including **FCCBs and FCEBs**. Money from non-residents against **non-convertible preference shares or debentures** (after 30 April 2007) is **ECB**.

**Not ECB**: **trade credit up to three years**, **export advances**, and investments received under the **debt and non-debt instrument rules**.

payload.title: How much can a company borrow abroad? The two-test limit
payload.core_explanation_md:
The borrowing limit is the **higher of two tests**:

1. **Outstanding ECB** up to **USD 1 billion**; or
2. **Total outstanding borrowing** (external **and** domestic) up to **300% of net worth** (last audited standalone balance sheet).

**Counts**: the **proposed** ECB (except refinancing). **Does not count**: **non-fund-based** credit and funds from **mandatorily convertible** securities.

**Exempt from the limit**: borrowers regulated by a **financial sector regulator**.

**Route**: all ECBs that meet the Schedule's parameters can be raised under the **automatic route** (subject to reporting); everything else goes to RBI under the **approval route**.

payload.title: Maturity and cost: three years, and market pricing
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Minimum average maturity period (MAMP): three years.**
- **Manufacturers** may borrow with an average maturity between **one and three years**, provided such ECBs outstanding stay within **USD 150 million**.
- **Call and put options** cannot be exercised before the MAMP is complete.
- **MAMP does not have to be met** on: conversion to equity or other non-debt instruments; repayment from **non-debt instrument proceeds** received after drawdown on a repatriation basis; **refinance**; **waiver** of debt by the lender; or repayment needed for **closure, merger, demerger, liquidation** and similar actions.

**Cost of borrowing** (interest, fees, expenses, guarantee fees, export credit agency charges, but **not commitment fees or Indian statutory taxes**): **in line with market conditions**.
- Under-three-year ECBs must stay within the **trade credit cost ceiling** (and for a fixed rate loan the swap-based floating rate plus spread must not exceed it).
- **Related-party** ECBs must be at **arm's length**.

payload.title: What ECB money cannot be used for
payload.core_explanation_md:
Barred end-uses in India (Regulation 3A), in a mnemonic of **"chit, Nidhi, land, farm, plant, TDR, shares, old loans, on-lending"**:

- **Chit funds** and **Nidhi** companies.
- **Real estate business** and **farmhouses** (with exceptions for construction-development projects and **industrial parks** that meet the conditions).
- **Agriculture and animal husbandry**, except floriculture, horticulture and vegetables under controlled conditions, seeds, animal husbandry, aquaculture and related services.
- **Plantation**, except **tea, coffee, rubber, cardamom, palm oil and olive oil trees**.
- **Trading in TDRs**.
- **Transacting in listed or unlisted securities**, except specified **strategic corporate actions** (merger, demerger, acquisition of control and similar).
- **Repaying a domestic rupee loan** that was used for a barred purpose or is an **NPA**.
- **On-lending** for any barred purpose.

payload.title: After the loan is agreed: LRN, proceeds, security, reporting
payload.core_explanation_md:
1. **LRN first**: draw down only **after** the Reserve Bank gives a **Loan Registration Number** through the **designated AD Category I bank** (Form ECB 1).
2. **Proceeds**: rupee spending money must reach an **Indian rupee account** by the **end of the next month**; waiting funds may sit in an **unencumbered fixed deposit up to one year**. Foreign currency spending money may stay in a **foreign currency account** in India or abroad.
3. **Security**: charge on assets or a **guarantee** under the Guarantees Regulations 2026; the loan agreement must carry the clause; **existing lenders' no objection** for encumbered assets; **RBI-regulated entities cannot guarantee**.
4. **Reporting**: **Form ECB 2** within **seven calendar days from the end of the month** of any drawdown or servicing; **Revised Form ECB 1** within seven calendar days from the end of the month in which a change took effect. A **late submission fee** regularises delay.
5. **Untraceable** borrowers: no returns for **four consecutive quarters** and cannot be found; the bank tells **RBI and the Directorate of Enforcement**.

Also allowed: **refinancing** (without breaking the original MAMP) and **conversion into equity** with the lender's consent and no extra cost.

payload.title: Trade credit for imports: amount, period, lenders
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Trade credit** is import-related credit from **outside India**. Under Schedule II of the Borrowing and Lending Regulations:

- **Amount**: up to **USD 50 million equivalent per import transaction**.
- **Period** (from the date of **shipment**): **one year, linked to the operating cycle**, for **non-capital goods**; **three years** for **capital goods**.
- **Currency**: any freely convertible currency, or **rupees**.
- **Lenders**: overseas **suppliers**, **banks and financial institutions**, **foreign equity holders**, and **IFSC** institutions.
- **Guarantees**: authorised dealers may issue **bank guarantees** in favour of the overseas supplier, bank or institution if the import and the credit comply with the norms.

Credits **up to three years** are **not ECB**: that is why trade credit sits under its own schedule.

payload.title: Does the proposed ECB fit the limit?
payload.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: an unregulated manufacturing company has net worth of USD 600 million. It has outstanding ECB of USD 900 million and other domestic borrowings of USD 400 million, and wants to raise a further USD 200 million of ECB (a new ECB, not a refinancing). Is it within the limit?

worked_steps.description: Test (a): outstanding ECB including the proposal, against USD 1 billion.
Test (b): 300% of net worth is the ceiling on total external plus domestic borrowing.
Total borrowing after the proposal: ECB plus domestic.
The limit is the higher of the two tests, so the borrower may use whichever it passes.

payload.final_answer_with_unit: The proposal fits: it fails the USD 1 billion test but passes the 300%-of-net-worth test (USD 1,500 million against USD 1,800 million), and the limit is the higher of the two

self_check.prompt_text: What is the largest total ECB this borrower could raise under test (b), given USD 400 million of domestic borrowing?
self_check.expected_takeaway: USD 1,400 million: 1,800 less 400 of domestic borrowing, which means a further USD 500 million on top of the USD 900 million outstanding.

payload.stem_md: A company (not regulated by a financial sector regulator) has net worth of USD 450 million, outstanding ECB of USD 300 million and domestic borrowings of USD 600 million. Under the limit based on net worth, what is the largest additional ECB it can raise, in USD millions? (Ignore the USD 1 billion test.)
payload.correct_explanation_md: 300% of net worth is 1,350. Total outstanding is 300 + 600 = 900. Headroom is 1,350 − 900 = 450.

payload.stem_md: A borrower asks which ECB maturity rule applies for a loan with a loan registration number obtained in May 2026. What is the position?

options.text_md: Three, five, seven or ten years depending on use
options.explanation_md: That is the earlier framework.

options.text_md: A minimum average maturity of three years, with a one-to-three-year option for manufacturers within USD 150 million
options.explanation_md: This is the framework in force after 16 February 2026.

options.text_md: One year for every borrower
options.explanation_md: Only manufacturers may use a shorter maturity, within a cap.

options.text_md: Whatever the lender and borrower agree
options.explanation_md: A minimum average maturity applies.

payload.correct_explanation_md: After the February 2026 amendment the MAMP is three years, with a one-to-three-year option for manufacturers whose such ECBs outstanding stay within USD 150 million.

payload.stem_md: A company with an investigation for a FEMA contravention pending against it wants to raise ECB. What is the position?

options.text_md: It is barred until the investigation ends
options.explanation_md: The amendment permits it with disclosure.

options.text_md: It may raise ECB only under the approval route and without disclosure
options.explanation_md: Disclosure is required.

options.text_md: It may raise ECB only in rupees
options.explanation_md: No currency restriction applies.

options.text_md: It may raise ECB, without prejudice to the outcome, but must disclose the pending matter in Form ECB 1
options.explanation_md: This is the rule.

payload.correct_explanation_md: A borrower facing a pending investigation, adjudication or appeal may still raise ECB, notwithstanding it, but must disclose it in Form ECB 1.

payload.stem_md: Which of these is NOT an ECB?

options.text_md: A floating rate note issued abroad
options.explanation_md: This is a form of ECB.

options.text_md: An FCCB
options.explanation_md: FCCBs are included in ECB.

options.text_md: Trade credit with an original maturity up to three years
options.explanation_md: Trade credit up to three years is excluded from ECB.

options.text_md: Money received from a non-resident against non-convertible debentures after 30 April 2007
options.explanation_md: Such funds are treated as ECB.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Trade credit with original maturity up to three years, export advances and certain investments are not ECB; FCCBs, FCEBs, notes and non-convertible debenture funds from non-residents are.

payload.stem_md: What is the ECB borrowing limit for an eligible borrower under the February 2026 framework?

options.text_md: The higher of outstanding ECB up to USD 1 billion and total outstanding borrowing up to 300% of net worth
options.explanation_md: This is the limit.

options.text_md: USD 750 million a year under the automatic route
options.explanation_md: That was the earlier framework.

options.text_md: USD 50 million per transaction
options.explanation_md: That is the trade credit limit per import.

options.text_md: USD 150 million
options.explanation_md: That is the cap on short-maturity manufacturing ECBs.

payload.correct_explanation_md: The limit is the higher of outstanding ECB up to USD 1 billion and total outstanding borrowing up to 300% of net worth, and it does not apply to borrowers regulated by financial sector regulators.

payload.stem_md: For which purpose may ECB proceeds be used in India?

options.text_md: Investment in a Nidhi company
options.explanation_md: Nidhi companies are barred.

options.text_md: Purchase of machinery for a manufacturing unit
options.explanation_md: Machinery for a manufacturing unit is not barred.

options.text_md: Trading in transferable development rights
options.explanation_md: TDR trading is barred.

options.text_md: Repaying a domestic rupee loan that is an NPA
options.explanation_md: Repaying an NPA loan is barred.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Machinery for manufacturing is not a barred end-use; chit funds, Nidhi companies, real estate business, TDR trading and repayment of NPA or restricted-use loans are.

payload.stem_md: When must an ECB borrower file Form ECB 2 after receiving proceeds or servicing the debt?

options.text_md: Within seven days of the transaction date
options.explanation_md: The period runs from the end of the month.

options.text_md: Within 30 days of the end of the quarter
options.explanation_md: This is not the period.

options.text_md: Before the drawdown
options.explanation_md: Form ECB 1 and the LRN come before drawdown; Form ECB 2 reports after.

options.text_md: Within seven calendar days from the end of the month in which the event took place
options.explanation_md: This is the reporting period.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Form ECB 2 is filed within seven calendar days from the end of the month in which the proceeds were received or debt servicing was undertaken.

payload.stem_md: ECB proceeds meant for rupee expenditure in India are drawn on 10 March 2026. By when must they be credited to a rupee account with the designated bank in India?

options.text_md: 31 March 2026
options.explanation_md: That is the end of the month of receipt.

options.text_md: 10 April 2026
options.explanation_md: That is one month after receipt.

options.text_md: 30 April 2026
options.explanation_md: The end of the succeeding month.
That is too late.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Proceeds for rupee expenditure are credited to a rupee account in India by the end of the succeeding month, which for a March receipt is 30 April.

payload.stem_md: What is the maximum amount of trade credit an importer can raise per import transaction under the regulations?

options.text_md: USD 1 billion
options.explanation_md: That is the ECB outstanding limit.

options.text_md: USD 50 million equivalent
options.explanation_md: This is the limit.

options.text_md: USD 5 million
options.explanation_md: That is the ceiling for advance remittance without a guarantee.

options.text_md: USD 150 million
options.explanation_md: That is the cap for short-maturity manufacturing ECBs.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Importers can raise trade credit up to USD 50 million equivalent per import transaction.

payload.stem_md: For how long, from the date of shipment, can trade credit be taken for import of capital goods?

options.text_md: Up to three years
options.explanation_md: This is the maximum for capital goods.

options.text_md: Up to one year linked to the operating cycle
options.explanation_md: That is for non-capital goods.

options.text_md: Up to five years
options.explanation_md: No such period applies.

options.text_md: Up to six months
options.explanation_md: That is the standard period for settling normal import payments.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Trade credit for capital goods can be for up to three years from the date of shipment, and for non-capital goods up to one year linked to the operating cycle.

payload.stem_md: Which of the following does NOT require the minimum average maturity period to be met?

options.text_md: Early repayment simply because the borrower has surplus cash
options.explanation_md: No such exemption exists.

options.text_md: Exercise of a put option in the first year
options.explanation_md: Options cannot be exercised before the MAMP.

options.text_md: A voluntary prepayment to reduce interest
options.explanation_md: No such exemption exists.

options.text_md: Repayment needed for a merger of the borrower
options.explanation_md: Repayment for corporate actions such as merger is exempt.

payload.correct_explanation_md: The MAMP need not be met for conversion, repayment from non-debt instrument proceeds, refinance, waiver of debt and repayment required for corporate actions such as merger, closure or liquidation.

unresolved: The courseware (printed pp. 166-170) describes the 2018-2019 ECB framework (MAMP of 3/5/7/10 years, all-in-cost ceiling, USD 750 million automatic route, liability-equity ratio, FATF/IOSCO lenders). RBI amended the regulations on 9 February 2026 (Gazette 16 February 2026), before the 30 June 2026 cut-off; the items teach the amended framework and card D001 flags the difference. If IIBF's examination follows the courseware, items quoting the old figures may be expected; the items do not test them.
The annex illustrating how average maturity is computed (Annex I to the regulations) was not read and is not taught.

Trade credit cost ceiling: the regulation text states a spread of 250 basis points over the benchmark "or as prescribed by the Reserve Bank", while the courseware says 300 basis points (350 for LIBOR-transition credits); the spread is not tested.
The Master Direction on External Commercial Borrowings, Trade Credits and Structured Obligations was not retrieved; the regulations themselves are taught.
The RBI regulations page used is the text amended up to 16 February 2026; later amendments before the cut-off were not seen.
Reviewer for this batch is the authoring agent; no independent or human review.
